searchText: There is no ETH 2. There is a change in consensus engine at The Merge from Proof of Work to Proof of Stake. There are also a number of scaling solutions/mitigations in the works like state expiry, state network, and regenesis. We have been trying to remove the ETH2.0 terminology from the public docs, where did you see it? Can someone help me out with this? Here’s my question: https://ethereum.stackexchange.com/questions/109602/how-to-integrate-eip-2981-with-this-basic-erc-721-contract I’m trying to write a super basic contract for a 1 of 1 NFT that also has a royalty system to pay me every time it’s resold. The official ethereum page on stable coins says: > In 2010, someone bought 2 pizzas for 10,000 bitcoin. At the time these were worth ~$41 USD. In today’s market that’s millions of dollars. There are many similar regretful transactions in Ethereum’s history. Stablecoins solve this problem, so you can enjoy your pizza and hold on to your ETH. Could someone please explain how a stable coin helps to profit from the price increase of a token after selling it? I don’t really understand the example that quote is a bit of an oversimplification the example there you *could* set up a dai vault and put your ether in that and use the dai dollars you get to buy the pizza it's not just "having stablecoins" solves the problem of price volatility I think this is a poor example and could use an update. I *believe* what the author is trying to get at is that you can use a crypto-currency platform *either* for buying/selling stuff (like Pizzas) or you can use it for speculating on the future value of ETH. I don't think they are suggesting that you engage in some complex leverage position to buy a pizza. Why did the Ethereum node count drop so dramatically this week? *maybe* because of the chain split incident the other day hello, i was reading the yellow paper and had some questions. is this the right channel / server? This is a server to discuss about research & development of the core protocol, although as long as it pertains to the latter it's usually fine. So if your question is not already answered on Ethereum stackexchange/reddit/etc, I'd say to go ahead and ask 🙂 might have missed this in the paper, but is there anything stopping a miner from only including 1 transaction in a block (ie well under the block gas limit) to try and produce as many valid blocks as fast as possible and collect block rewards? Nothing stopping it and they don't even need to include one transaction, but leaving out transactions won't help them solve PoW any faster. They'd just be leaving money on the table by not collecting the inclusion fees from transactions. You do see empty blocks turn up fairly regularly which is when by chance the miner finds the PoW solution before they've finished processing transactions to add to the block. There's no reason for them to not just publish it. But as soon as they can they get transactions included and try to find the PoW solution for a full block because that earns them more. > but leaving out transactions won't help them solve PoW any faster hmm i don't understand this part. my understanding was that you can only start solving for the PoW solution _after_ processing the transactions and creating the new block header. hence processing less transactions => start solving PoW faster => create block faster. are you saying that the time to process transactions <<< solving PoW? so the extra time gained by leaving out transactions is inconsequential that's correct and it's depending on the setup it's actually not uncommon for empty blocks to be mined if a miner gets lucky in the very small amount of time it takes between getting a block over the network and when they've fully validated it they just mine an empty block on top of the previous block if the pow checks out Miners may wind up creating multiple blocks they try and find the PoW solution for - first an empty one which is as quick as possible to create, then one filled with the available transactions but if a higher paying transaction comes along before they've found the PoW solution they may create a different block again to include that. ah, makes sense, very cool. thank you both! 🙂

excerpts.author: neery1218
excerpts.content: might have missed this in the paper, but is there anything stopping a miner from only including 1 transaction in a block (ie well under the block gas limit) to try and produce as many valid blocks as fast as possible and collect block rewards?

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content:
Nothing stopping it and they don't even need to include one transaction, but leaving out transactions won't help them solve PoW any faster.  They'd just be leaving money on the table by not collecting the inclusion fees from transactions.

You do see empty blocks turn up fairly regularly which is when by chance the miner finds the PoW solution before they've finished processing transactions to add to the block.  There's no reason for them to not just publish it.  But as soon as they can they get transactions included and try to find the PoW solution for a full block because that earns them more.
